This is the first stop in the tour. It shows what `scaffold()` does when a
notebook starts, how to read the project's settings, and the helpers that
describe the project. Nothing here changes your data.

## scaffold()

Every notebook and script starts with these two lines. Watch the messages:
scaffold() finds the project root, loads `.env`, attaches the packages marked
`auto_attach` in `settings/packages.yml`, sources `functions/`, sets the
ggplot2 theme from `settings/scaffold.yml` (once; `scaffold.R` no longer sets
it again), and creates `framework.db` on the first run.

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(framework)
scaffold()
```

The notebook lives in `notebooks/`, but code now runs from the project root,
so relative paths such as `inputs/raw` work the same everywhere.

```{r}
getwd()
standardize_wd()
```

The helpers in `functions/bp_helpers.R` were sourced by scaffold(), so
`classify_bp()` is ready without `source()`.

```{r}
classify_bp(systolic = c(118, 126, 134, 150), diastolic = c(76, 78, 84, 95))
```

## Project overview

`status()` is the one-screen health check: project type, git, AI files, renv,
directories (`ok` or `lazy`), and connections. The `study` connection is the
shared database, and `analysis` is a local scratch database. This project has
no `.git` of its own (`fw new` skips `git init` inside an existing
repository), so the git section reports the enclosing
`framework-test-projects` repository and counts the commits touching this
project.

```{r}
status()
```

`project_info()` lists every configured directory and which `save_*()`
function writes where. Directories marked lazy are created the first time
something is saved there.

```{r}
project_info()
```

## Reading settings

`settings()` reads one value by dot path. Split files (here
`settings/connections.yml`) are merged in, so the path doesn't care which file
holds the value.

```{r}
settings("project_name")
settings("directories.outputs_figures")
settings("connections.databases.study.database")
```

A missing key returns `NULL`, or the default you pass.

```{r}
settings("analysis.alpha", default = 0.05)
```

`settings_read()` returns the whole merged configuration as a list. These are
its top-level sections.

```{r}
project_settings <- settings_read()
names(project_settings)
```

`settings_write()` writes a settings list back to YAML. To keep this project's
files untouched, this writes a modified copy of the merged settings to a
temporary file and reads it back.

```{r}
temp_settings <- file.path(tempdir(), "settings-copy.yml")

copy <- settings_read()
copy$analysis <- list(alpha = 0.01, primary_outcome = "systolic_bp")
settings_write(copy, temp_settings)

settings_read(temp_settings)$analysis
```

::: {.callout-note}
A copy of `settings.yml` itself wouldn't read back from the temp folder: its
split-file references (`settings/author.yml`) resolve relative to the file's
own folder.
:::

## Dates and times

`now()` returns an ISO 8601 timestamp with the time zone, handy for log lines
and file names.

```{r}
now()
```

## Creating notebooks and scripts

The notebooks in this project were made with `make_notebook()`, and
`scripts/build-analysis-data.R` with `make_script()`. New files get a
sentence-case title made from the name (`bp-exploration` becomes "Bp
exploration").
`stubs_list()` shows the templates they can use; a project `stubs/` folder
overrides these.

```{r}
stubs_list()
stubs_path()
```

In real use you'd call `make_notebook("name")` and the file lands in
`notebooks/`. A `dir` is relative to the project root, wherever you call from,
so this puts the demo files in `scratch/make-demo/` (gitignored) and removes
them afterwards. Look at the messages: the presentation is called a
presentation.

```{r}
sandbox <- "scratch/make-demo"

make_notebook("bp-exploration", dir = sandbox, overwrite = TRUE)
make_rmd("bp-report", dir = sandbox, overwrite = TRUE)
make_presentation("bp-update-slides", dir = sandbox, overwrite = TRUE)
make_script("refresh-extract", dir = sandbox, overwrite = TRUE)
list.files(sandbox)
```

The title in the new notebook's YAML comes from its name.

```{r}
head(readLines(file.path(sandbox, "bp-exploration.qmd")), 3)
unlink(sandbox, recursive = TRUE)
```

Your own default notebook template lives in Framework's settings folder.
`read_framework_template()` shows it; `write_framework_template()` and
`reset_framework_template()` change and restore it.

```{r}
cat(head(strsplit(read_framework_template("notebook"), "\n")[[1]], 12), sep = "\n")
```

## Global settings and the project registry

Framework keeps your defaults (author, packages, directories for new projects)
outside any project, in `fw_config_dir()`.

```{r}
fw_config_dir()
global <- configure_global()
global$author
```

`project_list()` is the registry of projects created on this machine. Look for
the five `framework-test-projects/R` projects. The `exists` column marks
registered folders that are gone, and the message names them so you can drop
them with `remove_project_from_config(id)`.

```{r}
registry <- project_list()
registry[, c("id", "path", "exists")]
```

`config_sync()` copies settings from the Python package and `fw` CLI folder
into R's. With `dry_run = TRUE` it only reports what it would copy.

```{r}
config_sync(dry_run = TRUE)
```

## Bringing an existing folder in: adopt()

`adopt()` turns a folder you already use into a Framework project by mapping
its folder names to Framework directories. This builds a throwaway folder in
the temp directory and adopts it, so look at the proposed mapping and the
settings it writes.

```{r}
old_project <- file.path(tempdir(), "old-bp-analysis")
unlink(old_project, recursive = TRUE)
for (folder in c("data/raw", "data/clean", "R", "figures")) {
  dir.create(file.path(old_project, folder), recursive = TRUE)
}

adopt(old_project, yes = TRUE)
adopted <- readLines(file.path(old_project, "settings.yml"))
cat(adopted[1:20], sep = "\n")
```

The adopted project gets the same `connections:` layout as a new one, so
`db_connect("framework")` works there once you run `scaffold()`.

```{r}
connections_at <- grep("^  connections:", adopted)
cat(adopted[connections_at:(connections_at + 5)], sep = "\n")
```

## After a clone: bootstrap()

`bootstrap()` is what you run after cloning a project to a new machine or
cluster. It creates missing folders (output folders stay lazy), sets up
`framework.db`, and lists what is left to do, such as `.env` variables the
settings actually use. Every step is safe to repeat; `packages = FALSE` skips
installs.

```{r}
bootstrap(interactive = FALSE, packages = FALSE)
```

## Project specs

New projects are built from a resolved spec. `spec_resolve()` merges layers
(your defaults plus any overrides) into the full spec, and `spec_check()`
validates it. This is what `fw new` and Framework Cloud send to R.

```{r}
spec <- spec_resolve(
  layers = list(list(type = "project_sensitive")),
  name = "demo-sensitive"
)
spec$type
names(spec$directories)
spec_check(spec)
```

## setup() and the retired GUI

The local GUI is retired. `gui()` only warns and points to Framework Cloud.

```{r}
gui()
```

`setup()` with no token creates Framework's global settings file if it's
missing. It already exists here, so this changes nothing. With a project
token from Framework Cloud, `setup("fw_...")` creates that project locally;
that needs Cloud and isn't run.

```{r}
setup()
file.exists(file.path(fw_config_dir(), "settings.yml"))
```

## Not run here

- `view(df)` opens a data frame in a browser viewer. Try
  `view(db_query("SELECT * FROM participant_summary", "study"))`.
- `new_project()`, `new_project_sensitive()`, `new_course()`,
  `new_presentation()`, and `project_create()` create real projects and add
  them to the registry. The `fw new` CLI is the same thing from the shell.
- `quarto_regenerate()` overwrites `_quarto.yml` files.

```{r}
#| eval: false
setup("fw_your_project_token")
new_project("bp-followup", "~/Projects/bp-followup", offline = TRUE)
```
